content: In a study, it was observed that individuals who had between four and nine sexual partners were at a higher risk of HIV infection. Among young men who have sex with men (MSM), 75% of those with acute HIV infection reported engaging in sexual activity under the influence of drugs or alcohol, compared to 31% of HIV-negative MSM. The risk of HIV infection doubled for MSM with a sexual partner five years older and quadrupled with a partner ten years older. Peer support and counseling play a critical role in supporting adolescents living with HIV, especially those in key populations. However, some community-level activities, such as collecting medications from primary healthcare clinics, may pose personal safety and legal risks. Anonymous reporting systems and unique identifier codes should be implemented to protect confidentiality, as name-based reporting can violate privacy. Needle and syringe programs must clarify eligibility requirements, and policy and legal barriers to service provision should be reviewed and amended. Until such laws and practices are changed, adolescents with HIV may require legal support following HTC. Access to education should never be linked to health status, and the education sector has a vital role in supporting adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV) in their school environments. A comprehensive education sector response to HIV includes five key components: (1) providing quality education to reduce vulnerability to HIV, (2) evidence-based curricula that build knowledge and skills for protective behavior, (3) training and supporting educators on HIV knowledge and communication skills, (4) implementing workplace policies to prevent violence, abuse, and discrimination, and (5) integrating school health programs, peer education, and life skills education. Practical recommendations include recognizing the presence of students living with HIV, ensuring privacy and confidentiality, and fostering links with other sectors to support HIV response planning and resource allocation. Treatment education is essential for increasing the uptake of HIV testing and counseling, improving understanding of antiretroviral therapy (ART), supporting adherence, and reducing stigma. Adolescents living with HIV should be empowered to make decisions about their healthcare, with the ultimate goal of self-management as they transition to adulthood. To increase the acceptability and uptake of services among adolescents, strategies include minimizing facility visits, offering services at convenient times, reducing waiting times, and providing adolescent-friendly spaces. Integration of clinical care, laboratory services, and pharmacy pickups can reduce the burden on patients and providers. The Teen Club initiative in Eswatini, established in 2006, empowers adolescents living with HIV to live positively and transition successfully into adulthood. The clubs provide emotional and educational support through structured activities, life skills training, and peer support. Monthly meetings include games, educational sessions, and discussions led by trained teen leaders. The program has been successful in fostering confidence, reducing stigma, and providing a safe space for adolescents to share experiences. In Namibia, a program focusing on adolescents aged 10–19 aims to improve the quality and uptake of HTC and post-test support services. The program emphasizes HTC as an entry point to prevention, care, and treatment services. In Mozambique, the HIV/AIDS Treatment Acceleration Project (TAP) integrated HIV counseling, testing, and treatment into youth-friendly sexual and reproductive health services. Peer educators living with HIV provided support to newly diagnosed individuals, and support groups were established to promote adherence and healthy living. The program achieved high retention rates and served as a model for scaling up HIV services nationwide. In Brazil, a pediatric HIV program established in 1987 has evolved into a comprehensive care model, integrating multidisciplinary teams to provide holistic care for children and adolescents living with HIV. These initiatives highlight the importance of tailored, adolescent-friendly approaches to HIV care, emphasizing confidentiality, peer support, and integration of services to address the unique needs of young people living with HIV.
